## Abstract

This report introduces the concept, prototype design, projected costs, and scientific goals of a mobile experiment for detecting geoneutrinos originating from uranium and thorium decay chains in the Earth’s mantle. This will constrain the planet’s radiogenic heat production and unearth its geochemical makeup. This design of a deep-ocean mobile neutrino experiment, which is not mirrored by any active or planned experiments, supports physics and geoscience’s goal of multi-modal data on the Earth’s internal composition and structure. Based on geoscientific studies, this design is expected to achieve a 50–100-fold reduction in crustal background compared to similarly sized continental detectors, thereby enabling direct measurements of mantle geoneutrinos. The multiple stereoscopic projections enabled by the detector’s unique mobility can map spatial variations in heat-producing elements within the mantle. Beyond discussing the design, we report on our collaboration’s most recent hardware developments in the active prototyping of this detector. We briefly highlight the potential multiuse and interdisciplinary nature of this detector.

## I Science Program: Synergy between Earth Sciences and High-Energy Physics

### I.1 Mantle geoneutrinos — chemical composition of the Earth — why Ocean-Bottom Neutrino Detector

Uranium and thorium serve as long-lived fuel sources for Earth’s internal engine, supplying the energy that powers the geodynamo, which in turn shields life on our planet. Forged in ancient stars and later incorporated into the forming solar system, these elements were ultimately passed on to Earth. The radiogenic elements that heat our planet from within are, in a real sense, residual stardust. Directly establishing how much of this stellar legacy remains sequestered inside Earth is a clear and fundamental question that sits at the intersection of particle physics and planetary science.

How much heat is generated within Earth by radiogenic decay remains a central unresolved problem in Earth science. The bulk of this heat comes from the decay of the isotopes potassium-40, uranium-238, and thorium-232, which emit antineutrinos (geoneutrinos) through beta decays in their respective decay chains. Measuring Earth’s geoneutrino flux provides the only direct method for constraining the planet’s radiogenic heat production [64].

The central objective of geoneutrino studies is to quantify the absolute value and spatial variation of the surface flux of electron antineutrinos and electron neutrinos—collectively termed geoneutrinos—originating from $\beta$ and $EC$ decays within the Earth. Once measured, this flux can be converted into an estimate of the abundance and spatial distribution of uranium and thorium inside the planet.

Uranium and thorium are refractory elements (they condensed from the solar nebula at high temperatures and in the same chondritic ratios, as evidenced by meteorites that acted as the raw materials for planets) and lithophile (they form bonds with oxygen and are preferentially incorporated into Earth’s silicate shell rather than its metallic core). As a result, they are enriched in the mantle and continental crust, with up to about 40% of their total inventory residing in the continental crust.

Segregation of the Earth core was controlled by the chemical behavior of elements. Elements with chemical affinities for iron and nickel partitioned into the gravitationally dense, immiscible metallic alloy that sink to form the core. Based on its size and seismological properties, it is recognized that the core ended up with a bulk density that is about 10% less than that of iron-requiring elements that bond with iron only under reducing conditions (e.g., H, C, O, Si, and S).

During core formation, the composition of the metallic alloys that segregated to build the core largely prevented these elements from being incorporated in substantial amounts [32]. Consequently, constraining Earth’s total budget of refractory elements places tight limits on acceptable compositional models of the planet and determines the amount of radiogenic heat available to power geodynamic activity (e.g. plate tectonics, volcanism, mantle convection, and geodynamo).

Mantle convection underpins many processes that may be unique to Earth, including crustal recycling, plate tectonics, a geodynamo that has operated continuously for four-plus billion years, a mantle that has been cooling over the same time span, and the existence of long-lived mantle structures (i.e., LLVP, Large Low Velocity Province, 1000 km tall structures anchored at the core mantle boundary [56, 38]).

The thermal history of the Earth remains poorly constrained [30, 52]. At the most fundamental level, we can ask whether the planet cooled rapidly from its initially high temperatures or instead experienced a slower, more incremental decline. Over the last few billion years, has Earth cooled at a rate of the order of 50–70 K per billion years, or at an even lower rate? If the deep interior lost a large fraction of its primordial heat relatively quickly (as a result of impacts and a weakly insulating lithosphere), then its present-day cooling behavior would be closer to an asymptotic profile.

Determining how much radiogenic fuel is stored within Earth enables us to better constrain the cooling history of the mantle. However, due to present uncertainties, models of the thermal evolution of the Earth still yield a wide spectrum of values for the amount of primordial and radiogenic heat remaining inside the planet. Earth is made up of two fundamentally distinct regions with starkly different properties. Much like the difference between a cast iron skillet and a ceramic trivet in a kitchen, the metallic core is an extremely efficient conductor of heat, while the overlying mantle acts as a strong thermal insulator. Consequently, Earth’s cooling history is governed by heating from below (the core), internal heat production (radioactive decay) and the rate at which heat escapes from the surface.

The rate of change in mantle temperature ( $dT_{M}/dt$ ) is determined by the balance between the production of radiogenic heat within the mantle, $h_{M}(t)$ and the loss of heat from the core and surface, $Q_{core}(t)$ and $Q_{surf}(t)$ , normalized by the specific heat of the mantle, CM.

$$ \frac{dT_{M}}{dt}=\frac{h_{M}(t)+Q_{core}(t)+Q_{surf}(t)}{C_{M}} $$

The most up-to-date estimates for these values are: a surface heat flux of 46 $\pm$ 3 TW, a core heat flux of 10 $\pm$ 5 TW, a radiogenic heat production of the mantle of 13 $\pm$ 6 TW, and a mantle specific heat of 1100 $\pm$ 100 J kg-1 s-1 [49, 63]. Based on inferred concentrations of K, Th, and U in the continental crust [76], its corresponding radiogenic heat production is $7\pm 1$ TW (denoted $h_{cont}(t)$ ).

Because the continental crust does not participate in mantle convection or in transporting heat from the deep interior of the Earth, the remaining 39 TW (after subtracting the continental share) are the focus of ongoing debate. In particular, there is uncertainty about the relative contributions of primordial heat and radiogenic heating to the share of the mantle of the Earth’s internal energy budget. Since these uncertainties (23%, 50% and 46%, respectively) are correlated, the covariance term in the numerator of equation 1 leads to a combined uncertainty of $>$ 100%. Future geoneutrino measurements are anticipated to significantly reduce uncertainties ( $\leq$ 15%) in both $h_{cont}(t)$ and $h_{m}(t)$ , making the core heat flux the primary unknown.

Earth has two sources of fuel: primordial and radiogenic. Primordial energy comes from the kinetic energy generated during accretion and the gravitational energy accompanying core separation. Radiogenic energy comes from natural radioactive decay. Earth’s production of radiogenic heat is mainly from 40K, 232Th, 238U and 235U (i.e., 99.5% in total), with a lesser amount from 87Rb and 147Sm (i.e., 0.5%). Electron antineutrinos, including geoneutrinos and those from nuclear reactors, are presently being detected by particle physicists in large detectors (0.3 to 20 kiloton), underground ( $\sim$ 1 to 2 km deep). The total geoneutrino flux of the Earth is estimated to be approximately 5 $\times$ 1025 $\bar{\nu}_{e}$ s-1 or on average about 9 $\times$ 106 cm-2 s-1 [63]. Each neutrino leaving Earth removes a portion of its radiogenic heat. The flux of geoneutrinos is proportional to the abundance and distribution of Th and U in the Earth. Despite their ghost-like nature, these particles, being nearly massless (i.e., $<$ 10-6 $\times\;m_{e}$ [10]) and charge-less, are nearly impossible to detect, given their interaction cross-section of $<$ 10-45 cm2 [86]. For $\mathcal{O}(0.1-1)$ MeV-scale reactor neutrinos and geoneutrinos, one would need approximately 1000 light years of lead to shield half of them. This means that these particles, once generated, effectively leave the Earth with their complement of decay energy and traverse the universe. Despite their elusive behavior, since 2005 particle physicists have detected about one electron antineutrino per 1019 that pass through their detectors [13].

Today’s detection technology for neutrino geophysics is strictly deployed on continental crust, with detectors sited either near the margins or deeper in the interior of the continents. Approximately 50% of the signal measured at these detectors comes from the closest 250 km of continental crust [59, 13, 26, 46, 85], while the remainder typically comes in sub-equal proportions from the rest of the continents around the world and from the mantle. Consequently, translating the geoneutrino flux into a concentration of U and Th in the Earth requires an accurate and precise model for either the abundance and distribution of U and Th in the crust or the mantle. Knowing one of these parameters allows us to calculate the other. Therefore, our models for determining the concentrations of U and Th in the Earth depend entirely on the geological models that we build for both the mantle and the crust. If instead we were to measure a geoneutrino flux in an oceanic setting, far removed from the continents (e.g., southern equatorial Pacific, some 3000 km away from South America, Australia and the core-mantle boundary), we could assess the “mantle only” flux from inside the Earth [45, 99].

Thus, this paper seeks, to a certain extent, to rejuvenate the original Hanohano idea and highlight the development over the past 20 years in this area.

### I.2 Current state of affairs

The original Hanohano concept included a high-energy physics program: deploying a kiloton-scale liquid scintillator detector at a 50–60 km baseline offshore from a nuclear power complex to perform precision reactor antineutrino oscillation measurements. This medium-baseline program targeted improved determinations of $\theta_{12}$ and $\Delta m^{2}_{21}$ and sensitivity to the neutrino mass ordering using fine spectral structure. That HEP objective is now essentially being delivered by JUNO, a 20-kiloton liquid scintillator detector at a $\sim$ 53 km baseline to the Taishan and Yangjiang reactors, designed for percent-level oscillation parameter precision and mass-ordering sensitivity. Consequently, the detector described here is application-specific: its primary mission is Earth science, namely isolating and measuring mantle geoneutrinos.

From a geoscience perspective, continental detectors have established geoneutrino observation and provided the first constraints on radiogenic heat production. However, at all continental sites the measured flux is dominated by the local and regional crust, and uncertainties in crustal composition and structure remain the leading systematic that limits inference on the mantle contribution [84].

JUNO will accumulate a large geoneutrino sample due to its mass, but, like KamLAND and Borexino, it is located on continental crust and near powerful nuclear reactors, so crustal uncertainties and reactor backgrounds will continue to limit direct access to the mantle signal. In contrast, a deep-ocean deployment at a mid-ocean site places the detector beneath oceanic crust that is both substantially thinner (typically 6–7 km versus 30–40 km for continental crust [66]) and significantly depleted in heat-producing elements [97]. These factors reduce the crustal geoneutrino contribution by roughly a factor of 50–100. Together with the large distance from nuclear reactors and the strong suppression of cosmogenic backgrounds at abyssal depths, this configuration is uniquely suited to isolating the mantle component of the geoneutrino flux.

The present concept refocuses Hanohano-like detector as a purpose-built, application-specific observatory for Earth’s interior: an ocean-bottom antineutrino detector optimized to measure the mantle geoneutrino flux and, by extension, Earth’s radiogenic heat budget. Moreover, the mobility of a deep-ocean, relocatable detector enables measurements at multiple locations, creating a first-order map of heat-producing elements within the mantle [83]. In addition, advancing this technology provides the humankind with a mobile antineutrino detection capability that can be useful in other applications. Much like the benefits gained from sending humans to the Moon, we have reaped substantial rewards from being the first to develop such groundbreaking technology.

This experiment thus provides the first geochemical map of Earth’s deep interior and the only quantitative estimate of the current global amounts of Th and U inside the planet. Seismological data indicate that Earth’s interior is heterogeneous, featuring large-scale structures such as LLVPs, which are revealed by seismic tomography as regions of anomalously low seismic wave velocities beneath the Pacific Ocean and Africa relative to the surrounding mantle [56, 38]. Their origin remains a subject of debate, with hypotheses ranging from the enrichment of heat-producing elements, such as uranium and thorium and accumulation of thermochemical material transported by downwelling mantle flow at the core-mantle boundary [65], to Moon-forming impactor as a source of Earth’s basal mantle anomalies [104]. By comparing geoneutrino fluxes originating from distinct mantle regions, the experiment can determine whether the spatial distribution of heat-producing elements aligns with seismic structures [83]. Alternatively, such spatial variations can be resolved from a single observation site by exploiting the angular information of incoming geoneutrinos [100].

## II Prototyping and test sites in the US and Japan

### II.1 Original Hanohano study

Two decades ago, a detailed engineering study for the Hanohano deep‑ocean detector demonstrated that a 10,000 m3 detachable, cylindrical anti‑neutrino instrument is technically feasible for mantle radiogenic heat measurements [57]. The preferred configuration is a portable detector cylinder mated to a separate support barge, with bathyscaphe‑like deployment driven by fluid buoyancy and a shore cable carrying fiber‑optic data and electrical power. Stability and staged filling were validated analytically and with a 1:50 pool model; ocean‑current envelopes and catenary cable‑lay were modeled; descent and ascent to roughly 4,000 m were each under an hour; and a practical Hawaiian shore landing was planned.

Key subsystems were prototyped and are directly applicable: oil‑buffered optical modules behind clear windows; localized high voltage at the sensor; neighborhood digitizers feeding fiber optics; and a simple tree network that sent all pulses to shore. Power came in at approximately 1 W per channel, with total system power under approximately 2 kW; battery‑only one‑year operation was marginal, so cabled power was preferred. Implosion risk was measured and mitigated, sympathetic implosions at close spacing were observed at sea, while inserting syntactic foam into instrument spheres reduced peak shock and prevented chain reactions. Communications at roughly 1 Gb/s over standard submarine fiber were well within practice. Costwise, the ship and barge portion accounted for about one fifth to one quarter of total project cost, a planning ratio that remains useful even though absolute amounts have changed.

### II.2 Tests at University of Hawai‘i

The ALOHA Cabled Observatory (ACO) is located approximately 100 km north of Oahu, Hawai’i [44]. The observatory, which is actually a collection of instruments at Station ALOHA 4.7 km below the sea surface, established communications and power connection with Oahu providing oceanographic data on June 6th, 2011. The current maximum power rating is 1.2 kW. The observatory has hydrophones for listening to the ocean and a camera for visual observation. Various oceanographic measurements are constantly recorded, including the dissolved oxygen content, salinity, temperature and current profile of the water. The data is communicated to land via a retired AT&T telephone cable between Station ALOHA and Oahu. The constant and long-term data from ACO will be analyzed to discover patterns of ocean circulation, ocean-atmosphere interactions, seismology, climate change and other oceanographic topics.

UH Manoa Physics is interested in a number of tests that are realizable through the ACO and on campus with oceanography engineering staff. In particular, they are able to run pressurized tests mimicking (and surpassing) the conditions at Station ALOHA. While seeking the funds to perform pressurized tests are ongoing, tabletop tests at ground level are being done on SiPMs (silicon photomultipliers) to test if SiPMs are a valuable new technology to incorporate in an ocean bottom detector. We are using a laser to photo-stimulate the SiPM and are interested in seeing what are compatible safeguards to increase the detector’s survivability.

#### II.3.2 Liquid scintillator performance at deep ocean temperature

A dedicated low-temperature performance study was conducted for a laboratory-based liquid scintillator pertinent to OBD [79]. The liquid scintillator consists of LAB (Linear Alkyl Benzene) and PPO (2,5-diphenyloxazole) as a fluor. The temperature of the liquid scintillator, contained within an airtight 100 ml stainless steel container, was regulated at either 20 ${}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ or 4 ${}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , with the latter selected to replicate deep-ocean conditions. Scintillation light was detected via a 2-inch photomultiplier tube positioned beneath the vessel’s transparent viewing window. Using Compton scattering from a 137Cs gamma source, the study evaluated the scintillation light output as a function of PPO concentration. The findings revealed that the light yield at 4 ${}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ is systematically higher than at 20 ${}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ across the entire tested concentration range. As clearly illustrated by the trend in Figure 4, cooling the scintillator to deep-ocean temperatures consistently enhances the light yield.

For the candidate OBD formulation near a PPO concentration of 3.0 g/L, the study reports an approximately 8.6% increase in scintillation response at 4 ${}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ relative to 20 ${}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , after accounting for the independently measured PMT temperature effect. A conventional detector concept is shown in Fig. 6. Outward-facing PMTs provide a muon veto, with the surrounding ocean water acting as the veto and shielding volume.

Buffer oil (BO) serves to attenuate backgrounds from radioactivity in PMTs and nearby structures, and to provide optical coupling between the LS volume and the inward-facing PMTs. While the LS solvent was selected as LAB, the BO composition required dedicated evaluation. BO should have high optical transmittance, a refractive index similar to the LS to minimize optical losses, and a density similar to the LS to reduce differential loads on the acrylic vessel. BO candidates were screened for transparency and density, then characterized via transmittance, refractive index, and density measurements [73].

The acrylic vessel holds LS internally and BO externally, and bears sustained loads due to any density difference between the two liquids. Polymeric materials such as acrylic can gradually deform under sustained stress (creep), potentially reducing long-term structural margin. The structural design established two requirements. First, the detector must operate safely and without damage over long-term measurements ( $\sim$ 10 years) under deep-sea conditions (low temperature and high hydrostatic pressure). Second, the design should maximize light collection efficiency, which governs energy and position resolution. The target light collection efficiency was set to 450 p.e./MeV, comparable to KamLAND [47], consistent with prior simulations demonstrating feasibility for mantle geoneutrino observations and discrimination among radiogenic heat models.

## III Direction-sensitive Geoneutrino Detection

### III.1 Directionality via a pattern-matching algorithm

The detection of geoneutrinos has been based on the IBD reaction (3). In this reaction, the outgoing neutron retains a correlation with the direction of the incident antineutrino. Due to the reaction kinematics, the neutron is emitted preferentially in the forward direction, such that the displacement between the positron interaction point (prompt signal) and the subsequent neutron-capture location (delayed signal) can, in principle, be used to infer the incoming antineutrino direction [93]. However, in standard liquid scintillators used in both existing and decommissioned geoneutrino detectors, the neutron undergoes a prolonged random walk before capture, which washes out this initial displacement and destroys the directional information [87].

In practice, this directional information can be enhanced by doping the scintillator with nuclei that have large neutron-capture cross sections, such as ${}^{6}\mathrm{Li}$ or Gd, which substantially suppress neutron diffusion before capture [87, 82]. Such directionality has already been demonstrated in several reactor neutrino experiments [43, 12]. Recently, an algorithm has been developed to enhance the angular sensitivity of neutrino detectors. The algorithm uses pattern matching to identify the source direction and has a theoretical basis for the fit it uses [103]. Although it was developed in the context of determining source direction for reactor antineutrinos and for segmented detectors, it can in principle be used for geoneutrino since the underlying detection mechanism is the same. The algorithm was also found to have a reasonable angular sensitivity even at low event counts [28]. This will enable the detector to identify distributed sources.

### III.2 Measurability of HPE abundances in LLVPs

Some sensitivity studies based on a 1.5-kt OBD configuration demonstrated the feasibility of measuring HPE abundances in LLVP regions via directional geoneutrino detection [100, 101]. In these works, the mantle outside the LLVPs was assigned HPE abundances typical of a depleted MORB-source reservoir [16], while the remaining mantle HPE inventory was concentrated entirely within the LLVP regions. The results showed that direction-sensitive detection at Pacific Ocean sites not only enables the discrimination of LLVPs, but also permits the inversion of their internal HPE concentrations, thereby constraining their radiogenic heat production.

Using the same Earth models as in [101], we evaluate the sensitivity to LLVP structures using a profile likelihood ratio test. Sensitivities are evaluated for both 1.5-kt and 17-kt OBD configurations, extending previous studies that focused exclusively on the 1.5-kt case. To calculate the median expected significance, we adopt the Asimov dataset approach based on the asymptotic formulae from [27]. The null hypothesis ( $H_{0}$ ) assumes a uniform radioactive distribution in the mantle, while the alternative hypothesis ( $H_{1}$ ) includes LLVP structures enriched in HPEs. For the heterogeneous scenario, two LLVP-like regions are modeled immediately above the core-mantle boundary (CMB): one beneath the Pacific Ocean with a radius of 35∘ and one beneath Africa with a radius of 40∘, both extending up to 1000 km in height and located at nearly antipodal positions. In both the homogeneous and heterogeneous cases, the crust is modeled using CRUST1.0 [55] to ensure a realistic treatment of the local geological structure. We consider both 1.5-kt and 17-kt OBD configurations and include realistic backgrounds such as reactor antineutrinos and detector backgrounds as reported in [79, 72]. Specifically, the detector backgrounds are set equivalent to KamLAND’s initial high-noise phase [36] to ensure a conservative assessment.

Figure 8 shows the expected exclusion significance of the homogeneous mantle hypothesis ( $H_{0}$ ) hypothesis as a function of detector exposure and angular resolution. The results for the 1.5-kt and 17-kt OBDs are depicted by dash-dotted and solid lines, respectively, with colors indexing different angular resolutions. The results indicate that finite angular resolution significantly improves the ability of a single detector to identify LLVP structures, which in turn enables studies of HPE concentrations within these structures. Also, the larger target mass of the 17-kt configuration substantially increases the geoneutrino event rate, thereby reducing the exposure time required to accumulate sufficient statistics and allowing a high confidence level to be achieved within the initial years of operation.

## IV Impact beyond geoscience

### IV.1 Supernova neutrino observation

In addition to detecting neutrinos originating from within the Earth, the proposed OBD detector would also be sensitive to neutrinos from a Galactic core-collapse supernova (CCSN) event, thus proving key insights into the supernova mechanism. Current 3D radiation-hydrodynamic CCSN simulations are able to template predicted neutrino signatures [22, 48, 74, 67, 53].The neutrino event rate for an OBD-like detector, assuming a supernova occurring within a distance of 10 kiloparsecs, would be of the order of several hundred neutrinos per second, surpassing the $\sim$ 19 neutrinos detected from SN1987A, the only supernova neutrino signal observed to date [42, 19, 11]. Such a high event rate would enable us to follow the stages of the core-collapse supernova process in real time, including a gradual rise to a plateau as material from the outer layers of the star accretes onto the proto-neutron star forming in the core, followed by a decay in neutrino emission as the star enters the Kelvin-Helmholtz cooling phase. An abrupt cutoff to the neutrino event rate seen by the detector would provide a clear signature of black hole formation.

Neutrino detection would also allow rare insight into the stellar core structure in the moments of core collapse, revealing the otherwise opaque core density profile and constraining the tenuously understood nuclear equation of state [24, 89, 91, 71, 70, 69, 68, 81, 94, 21, 77]. Stars with different core compactness are predicted to differ by several hundred events per second in peak neutrino rate, and the high event rate in the detector would enable discrimination between stellar progenitor models. Theoretical correlations between the magnitude of the peak luminosity seen by the detector and remnant properties may also allow for the inference of the mass of the residual neutron star formed by the event. Finally, the amplitude of the signal, which is sensitive to neutrino oscillation physics, may place constraints on the neutrino oscillation model and mass hierarchy. Neutrino-driven instabilities in the first seconds of CCSN will shape the late-time (day-to-years) morphology of the ejecta distribution [92, 90, 35].

This OBD would complement the detections of other existing and upcoming detectors such as Super-Kamiokande, DUNE, and JUNO when a Galactic supernova occurs. As there are uncertainties in and degeneracies between neutrino luminosity, oscillation model, and progenitor compactness, the detection of a supernova neutrino lightcurve within multiple detectors is essential to accurately characterizing and disentangling the physical information encoded in the neutrino signal.

The OBD will also be deployed in the southern hemisphere during its lifetime. This will be the only antineutrino detector capable of detecting SN neutrinos and geoneutrinos in the southern hemisphere.

### IV.2 High energy physics

The ability to vary the baseline over a wide range of distances in the far field (tens of kilometers) offers a unique opportunity to systematically map the oscillation probability space, a capability that has not yet been realized in existing experiments.

Current reactor experiments such as KamLAND, along with its ongoing KamLAND2 upgrade, face a ”blurry” baseline, as the effective distance is averaged over contributions from multiple reactors, limiting precision in the measurement of oscillation parameters [37]. A setup involving a single, isolated power reactor located near a shoreline, combined with measurements taken at various baselines, would provide a more controlled environment to probe fundamental neutrino oscillation physics. Such an experimental configuration could also offer sensitivity to physics beyond the Standard Model (SM). While the JUNO experiment, which has come online, will make significant contributions to the field, other detectors such as SNO+ face statistical limitations due to the large distances separating the reactor sources from the detector. Furthermore, none of the existing far-field land-based detectors are equipped to vary baselines, which constrains their ability to explore oscillation phenomena across a broader parameter space, without relying on the energy binning to effectively sample various $L/E$ values.

The OBD can in principle serve as a far detector in the long-baseline accelerator-neutrino context. The central advantage of a mobile deep-ocean far detector is the ability to choose and adjust the baseline (like in the reactor context) and off axis angle after the beam has been constructed. For fixed underground detectors, the baseline and off-axis angle are effectively locked in by geography and civil engineering constraints. In contrast, a relocatable deep ocean detector can be deployed at a range of baselines along the beam axis, and at selected off axis angles defined by available deep water locations, allowing detailed optimization of oscillation physics reach.

Baseline flexibility allows one to probe different oscillation maxima and matter effect regimes using the same beam and detector technology. For example, a Tokai-to-Kamioka (T2K) beam [1] aimed toward a deep ocean site at longer baseline (like in the proposed Tokai-to-Kamioka-Korea experiment [2]) could enhance sensitivity to mass ordering and subdominant CP violating effects by exploiting stronger matter effects over the longer path length. A mobile far detector could first be operated at one baseline to collect an initial data set, then redeployed to a second baseline to test degeneracies and cross check oscillation parameter fits with different $L/E$ coverage, without constructing a new cavern. This approach mirrors, at far detector scale, the “spectral shaping” concept that motivates a vertically moving detector, such as Intermediate Water Cherenkov Detector (IWCD) at the near site [80, 29], but now uses geographic relocation to tune the oscillation pattern.

Off-axis angle control provides additional leverage. As in the IWCD concept, the accelerator neutrino energy spectrum depends strongly on off-axis angle. While a far detector cannot scan angles continuously in the way a small near detector can, a mobile platform can be positioned at a discrete set of deep ocean sites that correspond to different off-axis angles, each providing a different beam energy spectrum. In principle, a sequence of deployments at selected angles could mimic narrower or broader spectra and provide complementary sensitivity to appearance and disappearance channels, or optimize the balance between event rate and energy resolution for CP violation studies.

A mobile deep-ocean detector can, beyond its scientific mission, drive next generation HEP technology R&D because it must operate at large scale with tight power and bandwidth constraints and only remote servicing. Those requirements motivate development of marine compatible scintillating media (and potentially enviromentally friendly detection media), including hybrid water-based scintillators [102, 54, 34], to improve low energy performance and particle identification; large area photosensors such as advanced SiPM arrays [75] and LAPPDs [8] to improve photon detection efficiency, timing, and spatial resolution relative to PMTs; highly integrated low power multi channel SoC readout electronics designed for pressure tolerant deep sea housings; real time data reduction and intelligent triggering using AI/ML on FPGAs and SoCs [39] to compress data in situ, identify rare signatures, and adapt to changing source and background conditions; and improved reconstruction and analysis algorithms, including ML-based event classification and energy reconstruction [58]. Many of these developments are of relevance to future HEP detectors, such as DUNE [31]. It also drives innovation in high-pressure enclosures, connectors, feedthroughs, and electronics packaging relevant to neutrino telescopes, such as IceCube [40] and KM3NeT [60]. Because the detector is modular and relocatable, these technologies can be deployed, upgraded, and benchmarked across multiple campaigns, accelerating maturation for future underground and underwater detectors, long-baseline experiments, and other low power, high granularity autonomous sensing applications in harsh environments.

### IV.3 Nonproliferation and nuclear reactor monitoring capabilities

Although the primary motivation for an OBD is fundamental neutrino science, the system naturally offers a set of attractive capabilities for nuclear monitoring and nonproliferation applications. The key distinguishing feature is mobility: unlike large underground detectors, the OBD can be engineered as a relocatable asset that is deployed and recovered using standard marine operations. Once the detector technology and support infrastructure are in hand, this provides a standing capability that can be moved on timescales of months to specific regions of interest, including areas where terrestrial access is politically or logistically difficult. In practice, a small number of such instruments could, over time, survey an extensive geographic region by redeployment rather than new construction at each site.

From an infrastructure perspective, ocean bottom deployment avoids the need for excavation or the creation of large underground cavities, which has been a dominant cost and schedule driver for land-based detectors. The ocean water column provides a natural, uniform overburden, simplifying shielding requirements and decoupling the detector cost from site specific civil engineering. This architecture is inherently modular and extensible; additional scientific or application specific payloads, including seismometers, oceanographic sensors, or dedicated monitoring instruments, can be integrated into the same platform. As new monitoring modalities or analysis techniques are developed in the future, they can be incorporated into subsequent OBD deployments without re‑engineering a fixed underground site.

In the nonproliferation context, OBD is particularly relevant for monitoring coastal nuclear facilities and future ocean-based energy systems, such as floating nuclear power plants or maritime reactor platforms, for which an ocean coastline is effectively “closer” than any land border. Previous analyses have shown that allowing detector deployment at sea, at coastline rather than traditional land border distances, increases the number of facilities that are observable with finite detector masses [25]. At the 12 nautical mile territorial sea limit (about 22 km), even a relatively small 50-MW reactor produces of order 100 IBD events per kiloton per year, which is a meaningful signal level for long term monitoring. The OBD capability positioned just outside territorial waters can therefore provide a unique, non‑intrusive complement to traditional monitoring tools in selected cases, especially where direct access on land is constrained.

At the same time, there are important limitations that shape realistic monitoring use cases. If the detector is optimized primarily for reactor monitoring, it will generally operate at depths and locations where reactor antineutrino flux dominates, which significantly complicates precision measurements of geoneutrinos. Moreover, when deployed near a continental margin, the local crustal geoneutrino flux dominates and the mantle contribution remains subdominant, which further limits sensitivity to global mantle properties [45]. Depth requirements for physics performance and background reduction also impose strong constraints on where the OBD can be deployed. Finally, the relevant legal and diplomatic frameworks, including the 12 nautical mile territorial sea definition and broader issues of operating scientific sensors near another state’s critical infrastructure, will constrain where and how such a system can be used. Taken together, these considerations imply that the OBD should be viewed not as a universal monitoring solution, but as a flexible, relocatable asset that can provide targeted, high-value neutrino-based information for a subset of coastal and maritime nuclear systems, as a “bonus” capability layered on top of their core scientific mission.

## V Conclusion

Up to this point, the understanding of Earth’s geochemical composition has relied entirely on surface sampling, seismology, and numerical simulations. Geoneutrinos change this. For the first time, real-time observation of the Earth’s interior chemical composition is possible by a method other than seismology. Neutrinos have become a mature probe of the Universe, from solar neutrinos to high-energy neutrino astronomy. By comparison, the Earth remains incompletely characterized in one of its most basic properties. These properties include the geochemical magnitude and distribution of radiogenic heating, which power thermal evolution, mantle convection, and plate tectonics. Since the first detection of geoneutrinos by KamLAND, with subsequent measurements by Borexino, SNO+, and the upcoming JUNO experiments, neutrino geoscience has demonstrated a direct, quantitative sensitivity to heat-producing elements. At the same time, present measurements are fundamentally limited by the continental crust contribution and its uncertainties. Currently, the mantle and bulk silicate Earth radiogenic power remain poorly determined, with published measurements spanning a wide range.

A deep-ocean, relocatable antineutrino detector provides a uniquely enabling next step. We can position the OBD in the middle of the Pacific, and thus sampling only the mantle, from about 3000 km away from the core and continents. Deployed far from continents, the measurement becomes mantle-dominated (the crust contribution becomes about 50–100 times suppressed compared to land-based detectors, substantially reducing an otherwise dominant crustal contribution that limits land-based experiments. This also means that this experiment will be far from nuclear reactors. Additionally, the deep-ocean environment offers strong shielding from cosmic-ray muons. Taken together this deployment choice provides superior background suppression. In this configuration, geoneutrino detection can evolve from demonstrating feasibility to delivering a definitive mantle measurement capable of discriminating competing models for Earth’s composition and heat budget.

In the past two decades, the field has advanced through improved geoneutrino statistics, multi-site measurement, and analysis maturity. In parallel, enabling technologies have progressed, including modern photosensors and low-power multi-channel electronics readout, improved calibration and simulation tool-chains, and data driven analysis, such as AI/ML methods. Beyond fundamental science, antineutrino detection is increasingly discussed in applied contexts, including remote monitoring, nonproliferation, and emerging maritime nuclear concepts.

Critically, ocean-bottom detection is no longer only a concept study. Recent work, including student research at University of Hawai’i and multiple theses at Tohoku University, has advanced key elements. This research includes background assessments, Geant4 simulations, directionality algorithms, prototype detector development, structural analyses, and dedicated measurements of liquid scintillator performance at deep-ocean temperatures. Planned near-term deployments of a prototype to multi-kilometer depth will directly address remaining questions about in situ performance under hydrostatic pressure and operational constraints.

We therefore propose a phased program to transform OBD design from concept to capability: (i) targeted R&D and at-sea prototype validation with deployment to mature operational sites such as the ALOHA Cabled Observatory, retiring the principal technical and operations risks, followed by (ii) design maturation and partnership development leading to (iii) a full-scale relocatable deep-ocean detector and a multi-site measurement campaign. By exploiting existing deep-ocean science sites with cabled power and data transference, we reduce cost and risk factors. When fully developed, OBD’s mobility will enable the acquisition of geoneutrino data at multiple ocean locations. The OBD can move beyond a single mantle-averaged constraint toward the first geoneutrino map of mantle radiogenic compositions, and provide the necessary data to test competing models for mantle composition and heat production. This program would establish a new observatory-class tool for both neutrino physics and Earth sciences, enabling mantle-focused geoneutrino measurements that are not achievable on land and open a pathway to transformative cross-disciplinary results.

## Abstract

The NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory will complete its ten-year Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) in the mid-2030s. Its 8.4 m aperture and 9.6 deg2 field of view give it an étendue unmatched by any facility planned for that era. The Rubin 2036: Opportunities for Discovery workshop (KIPAC/SLAC, 3–5 August 2026) brought together $\sim$ 100 participants to ask . This paper summarizes the workshop’s structure and discussions. Five working groups considered continued LSST-style surveying; alternative cadences and footprints; new filters; targets of opportunity and multi-messenger astronomy; and enabling technologies and upgrades. The continued-surveying group explored for detection, deblending, and classification in the faint, crowded sky. The cadence group described a process for allocating post-LSST observing time, along with cadences for a transiting-exoplanet census, Type Ia supernova cosmology, time-delay cosmography, and second-scale transients. The filter group explored offset broadband, medium-band, and narrowband filters for photometric redshifts, high-redshift large-scale structure, AGN reverberation mapping, Galactic archaeology, and emission-line imaging. The multi-messenger group explored target-of-opportunity follow-up of next-generation gravitational-wave and neutrino sources, including standard sirens, kilonovae, and Galactic supernovae. The technology group organized instrumental options by cost and lead time, from configuration changes such as fast readout modes to moderate upgrades such as new filters, a faster shutter, and summit edge computing. Cross-cutting topics included AI/ML, Chilean and Latin-American co-leadership, satellite megaconstellations, and weather and long-term climate trends at Cerro Pachón. The working groups’ white papers are available through the workshop’s Zenodo community (https://zenodo.org/communities/rubin2036workshop/) and the workshop website, which also includes workshop talks (https://rubin-observatory.github.io/Rubin-Beyond-LSST/pages/Rubin2036proceedings/).

## I Introduction

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory was designed and built to carry out the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST): a decade-long, optical survey of the southern sky in six broad photometric bands ( $ugrizy$ ) [23, 9]. The four science pillars of the LSST are probing dark energy and dark matter, taking an inventory of the Solar System, exploring the transient sky, and mapping the formation and structure of the Milky Way. The LSST began in 2026, and by the mid-2030s the nominal ten-year survey will be complete, delivering an unprecedented $\sim$ 18,000 deg2. The telescope, camera, data-management system, and the software will remain one the most capable wide-field imaging worldwide.

It presents for Rubin operations beyond the LSST, built on concrete science cases that the community could develop for upcoming prioritization processes, including the next decadal survey in astronomy and astrophysics (Astro2030).

The scientific cases for Rubin rely on its unique étendue ( $A\!\cdot\!\Omega$ , the product of collecting area and field of view). No facility planned for the 2030s will match Rubin’s combination of an 8.4 m aperture and a 9.6 deg2 field of view. Other imaging and spectroscopic facilities, such as the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), the 4-meter Multi-Object Spectroscopic Telescope (4MOST), the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope (Roman), and Euclid, will provide complementary capabilities. By the mid-2030s we will also have of data products and scientific discoveries enabled by the LSST itself.

Continuing to operate and evolve a built facility a high-return use of resources: the marginal cost of new capability is small relative both to the cost already committed and to any new facility of comparable reach.

Over the past decade a series of community studies has argued for planning Rubin’s use beyond the LSST, from the Cosmic Visions Dark Energy reports [18, 19, 17], through Astro2020 white papers on next-generation LSST science and future uses of the facility [24, 26], the LSST next-generation instrumentation workshop [34], dedicated narrow-band filter studies [36], and the Snowmass 2021 process [12, 21, 6] (see Appendix D for a summary of previous work). ## II Group A: Continued LSST-style Surveying

Contributors: P. Yadav. See Yadav [35] for the full Group A document.

Group A considered continuing to survey with the current system beyond the nominal ten years, gaining scientific reach from a longer time baseline, and deeper coadds rather than from any new hardware . Its case argues that the deeper, more crowded imaging a continued survey produces can only be exploited if the detection, deblending, and classification software evolves in step, an argument for sustained investment in rather than in the itself.

### II.1 A survey-native foundation model for the faint, crowded sky

A continued, deepening survey if its faint, crowded sky can actually be measured, and at those depths the fraction of blended detections rises steeply while the availability of vetted training labels does not. The central question is whether a survey-native foundation model (a backbone pretrained self-supervised on Rubin’s own unlabeled $ugrizy$ coadds) can deliver scene-level detection, deblending, and star/galaxy classification at the faint end using only a small fraction of the labels that supervised training requires. The single result that would matter is matching fully supervised performance from roughly 5–15% of the labels, making a scene-level catalog deployable across the whole footprint rather than only in the handful of spectroscopically rich deep fields. The $A\!\cdot\!\Omega$ argument here is two-sided: the same survey depth that drives fields into the blended regime (where morphology-only star/galaxy separation degrades to $\sim$ 50% correctly classified injected stars at $i=23.8$ in Data Preview 1 (DP1) source-injection tests) also guarantees that unlabeled pixels, unlike vetted labels, scale exactly with $A\!\cdot\!\Omega$ . Evidence from the first application of the DeepDISC scene-level framework to real LSST DP1 imaging (1,458 six-band tiles over the Extended Chandra Deep Field South and the Euclid Deep Field South; 288,277 objects, validated against the Hubble Space Telescope and the Cosmic Assembly Near-infrared Deep Extragalactic Legacy Survey) shows scene-level inference reaching 94.8%/71.4% galaxy/star recall against HST (near-parity with a photometry-based random forest) while achieving 94.6% catalog purity on a held-out HST footprint versus 77.6% for the Scarlet-based production pipeline on the same sky. The requirement is not telescope time but infrastructure: sustained GPU compute and bulk-image access for data-release-scale pretraining ( $\sim$ 2–3 yr to stand up), a deep-field truth program (source-injection plus curated spectroscopic/astrometric labels, coordinated with DESI/4MOST), and an integration path to release scene-level catalogs as supported value-added data products. The priors, rerunning the $i=23.8$ injection benchmark with image-based classifiers and , are obtainable from Data Preview 2 (DP2) and . This case , connecting to Roman (joint pixel-level training cuts the simulated unrecognized-blend fraction from 18.6% to 11.6%), Euclid, DESI and , and to Groups B (which deep fields exist to train on), C (photo-z quality is bounded by blended-photometry quality), D (host identification in crowded fields), and E (compute/software infrastructure). A Chilean co-leadership tie-in was proposed around the truth/label program and a data-science training-school module.

Group B addressed how to re-tune Rubin’s observing strategy after LSST (e.g., denser cadence, mini- and sub-surveys, monitoring programs, and target-of-opportunity splits) to reach science that the homogeneous, compromise-driven main-survey cadence cannot. Group B participants also identified a “metacase” for the workshop at large: a proposal that the community establish a flexible, prioritized process for allocating post-LSST observing time, rather than commit now to a single fixed alternative cadence. Around that umbrella the group developed a set of concrete science-driven cadences.

### III.1 The metacase: a process for the post-LSST science portfolio

The observation motivating the metacase is that Rubin’s capabilities are not exhausted by the LSST survey design: survey-cadence proposals have consistently oversubscribed the available LSST time, and new ideas as the survey progresses. Because cadence and footprint changes have (shorter than filters or focal-plane hardware), they . What Rubin needs is a survey-strategy framework that can run concurrent programs of differing scale, area, filter set, exposure time, and cadence, together with a scientific prioritization process, modeled on the large/medium/small proposal structure used at other observatories (e.g., Roman’s mix of core community surveys and proposal-based general-astrophysics surveys). The counterargument that the LSST cadence was already optimized in a community process is answered by noting that the most important science in 2036 will differ from the original LSST science goals, and that the main survey necessarily compromised across all cases rather than serving finely targeted ones. Success would be measured by the number and oversubscription of proposals received and by the breadth of community participation; a Chilean tie-in (reserved Chilean-community time or a Chilean Time Allocation Committee, TAC) is a natural component. The metacase is the umbrella under which most Group B, and several cross-group, cases sit.

### III.2 Science-driven cadences

The group developed several cases that such a process would prioritize:

#### Transiting-exoplanet census of the Milky Way disk

A census of transiting planets across all spectral types in the Galactic disk, confirming candidates through $\geq 3$ transits, over $\sim$ 3,600 deg2 of the disk. It requires operational flexibility rather than hardware: . Kepler (0.25% of sky) and the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS; bright stars, $r\lesssim 12$ ) leave most of the disk’s planet population unprobed; a benchmark target is confirming planets around $\geq$ 10,000 disk stars.

#### Young stellar objects across all timescales

A multi-band ( $ugriz$ ), high-cadence (30-minute), short-duration ( $\sim$ 10-day) sub-survey of thousands of young stellar objects (YSOs) in several star-forming regions of Rubin’s Galactic footprint would link short-term accretion bursts to long-term eruptive events such as those of EXor-type stars (young stars that undergo repeated months-to-years-long accretion outbursts). Exploiting Rubin’s étendue and its blue and red filters, it would recover light-curve morphologies, determine stellar photospheric properties, and characterize accretion physics as a function of stellar age and environment. Its complementarity with the low-cadence, multi-year LSST view uniquely constrains the occurrence rates of small- versus large-scale events in the accretion histories of young stars, extending the YSO micro-survey already proposed for the LSST [13].

#### Type Ia supernova cosmology to $z\sim 1.1$

A dedicated sub-survey drilling into non-Deep-Drilling-Field regions to fill the Hubble diagram out to $z\sim 1.1$ , where the ten-year LSST sample is sparse, tests of time-varying dark energy beyond $(w_{0},w_{a})$ and tests of cosmic isotropy along continuous sightlines. It needs no new filters; Group C’s offset filters would most benefit this case by preserving discovery depth. Mid-to-late-release cosmology results are the prior that would set the strategy.

#### Strongly-lensed AGN and supernovae for time-delay cosmography

Daily cadence on $\sim$ 2,000 deg2, preferentially on the Roman high-latitude footprint, to measure time delays of lensed quasars and the rare, rapidly-fading lensed supernovae. Concrete performance metrics include accretion-disk sizes measured to 10%, a $5\sigma$ discrimination , and 1% $H_{0}$ from each of the lensed-SN and lensed active-galactic-nucleus (AGN) samples.

#### The few-second sky: ultracompact binaries and fast transients

Two cases exploit second-scale cadence. A fast-cadence Galactic survey (1–2 s continuous imaging over an hour, repeated over years) targets Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA)-era eclipsing double white dwarfs with sub-15-minute periods, comparing the optically-timed orbital decay $\dot{P}$ against the gravitational-wave (GW)-driven prediction to isolate tidal dissipation and test whether such binaries are calibrated GW sirens, a measurement whose precision scales as $\sim T^{-5/2}$ , so . A complementary extragalactic case targets fast blue optical transients and fast-radio-burst (FRB) counterparts, which are washed out in a standard 30 s visit and require 1–2 s readouts plus second-scale alerting. Both depend on enabling technology from Group E (fast readout modes).

#### Solar-System and coordinated-observing mini-surveys

An ecliptic-restricted, daily-cadence mini-survey pairing $g$ and $r$ within each visit would catch the rise of cometary and active-asteroid outbursts and distinguish dust- from gas-driven activity by color; and a framework for commensal or simultaneous observing with other facilities (the Dark Energy Camera, DECam; the Southern Astrophysical Research Telescope, SOAR; the Very Large Telescope, VLT; LS4; radio: Simons Observatory, the Atacama Cosmology Telescope, ACT; the Square Kilometre Array, SKA) would enable science requiring same-time multi-wavelength coverage (explicitly excluding multi-messenger triggers, which are Group D’s domain).

A recurring observation was that essentially every proposal costs of order one to a few million dollars per filter, a small marginal cost on an existing facility. The unifying proposed was the ratio $R(T,)=\mathrm{FoM}(\text{new filter set})/\mathrm{FoM}(ugrizy)$ at fixed time $T$ and . The seven cases below are summarized here; each is developed in full, with quantitative forecasts, figures, and references, in the group’s detailed document [11].

### IV.1 Cosmology and extragalactic science

#### High-redshift large-scale structure with medium bands

The goal is to measure high-redshift large-scale structure using Lyman- $\alpha$ emitters (LAEs) at $z\gtrsim 2$ selected with medium-band filters, together with LSST-selected Lyman-break galaxies (LBGs) refined by medium-band photometry, and to perform a $2\times 2$ -point analysis (LAE/LBG clustering $\times$ cosmic microwave background, CMB, lensing) constraining $\Omega_{M}$ , $S_{8}$ , neutrino mass, and $(w_{0},w_{a})$ with the longest available lever arm, while accessing primordial-Universe physics ( $f_{\rm NL}$ ) where structure is less nonlinear. The headline figure of merit is a forecast $\sim$ 4–5% constraint on $\sigma_{8}$ per medium band from the LAE clustering $\times$ Simons Observatory CMB-lensing cross-correlation, well beyond existing measurements at this redshift. Only Rubin can detect LAEs and enable clean LBG selection over the $\geq$ 11,000 deg2 that Spec-S5 requires: , the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope (CFHT) has a much smaller , and Subaru/Hyper Suprime-Cam (HSC) surveys $\sim$ 3 $\times$ more slowly and is not survey-dedicated. The concrete need is a minimal set of $\sim$ 7 medium bands with $\lambda/\Delta\lambda\sim 20$ spanning $2.1\lesssim z\lesssim 3.5$ with continuous coverage (LAE wavelength–redshift mapping: 400 nm $\rightarrow z=2.3$ ; 700 nm $\rightarrow z=4.8$ ), at $\sim$ $1M per filter, ideally reaching $2<z<6.5$ with Roman supplementing the high end. Current target-selection efficiency with plus HSC broadbands is already 75% against DESI. The case connects tightly to the Simons Observatory (SO; which supplies the CMB-lensing map), DESI, and the Prime Focus Spectrograph (PFS), and, most importantly, to Spec-S5, whose LAE sample requires $\sim$ 4 years of Rubin dark-time medium-band observing as a precursor: the two facilities should be optimized jointly. The precursor HSC-Niji survey (medium bands binned into four “quadrants” MBQ1–4 to avoid slow filter exchanges; MBQ1 delivered in 2025) demonstrates the approach, and photo- $z$ forecasts indicate that adding $\sim$ 16 medium bands to the six broad bands meets LSST Year 1 (Y1; and largely Year 10, Y10) weak-lensing and large-scale-structure (LSS) photo- $z$ requirements. The chief open question is quantify the marginal gain over LSST alone.

#### Offset broad bands for photometric redshifts

Rather than medium bands, this case adds a set of 5–7 broad bands offset in wavelength from $ugrizy$ , gaining spectral information (and thus better per-object photo- $z$ and high- $z$ target selection) while still retaining the depth needed for transient and proper-motion science that medium bands would sacrifice. The target is a factor of $\sim$ 2 reduction in photo- $z$ scatter and outlier rate, matching the gain expected from doubling spectral resolution and exposure time, at $1–2M per filter. An empirical test using the Cosmic Evolution Survey (COSMOS) 2020 catalog found that 11 offset broad bands outperform both the six-broadband and the twelve-medium-band scenarios in photo- $z$ scatter and outlier fraction, and a hybrid (six medium blue $+$ six broad) is nearly as good. Because it preserves time-domain science, this is regarded as the “workhorse” filter option; it connects to Spec-S5 target selection, CMB cluster surveys (South Pole Telescope, SPT-3G $+$ /SO), X-ray clusters (Athena), and radio weak lensing (SKA). The prior is synthetic photometry from COSMOS-class spectral-energy-distribution (SED) catalogs rather than new data.

#### AGN accretion-disk reverberation mapping and cosmology

Rubin will produce the largest homogeneous time-domain AGN sample ever assembled, turning continuum reverberation mapping from a targeted, single-quasar technique into a population-scale experiment across black-hole mass, accretion rate, and redshift. Medium bands ( $\lambda/\Delta\lambda\sim 15$ –20) placed to separate continuum-dominated from line-dominated spectral regions, on a $\sim$ 1–2 day cadence in the Deep Drilling Fields, would measure accretion-disk sizes and temperature profiles after removing redshift-dependent contamination, resolving the long-standing puzzle that measured disks are larger than thin-disk theory predicts. A contamination-controlled disk-size sample could in principle serve as a geometric cosmological ruler complementing Type Ia supernovae. A pilot would target continuum lags for several hundred AGN; the mature program, several thousand. The case has natural Chilean co-leadership through Rubin, Gemini-South, and SOAR, with the Southern Photometric Local Universe Survey (S-PLUS) and 4MOST-ChANGES as tie-ins.

#### Protocluster assembly

A companion extragalactic case seeks a complete catalog of protoclusters at $z<4$ , tracing when the highest-mass halos assemble and how their galaxies transform, using precise medium-band or variable-filter photometric redshifts and intracluster light as a mass proxy, building on Euclid, Euclid $\times$ LSST, and Sunyaev–Zel’dovich candidate lists (LSST broadbands alone reach only $z\lesssim 1.3$ –1.4).

### IV.2 Local-Universe, stellar, emission-line, and exotic-filter concepts

#### Galactic archaeology and local dark matter

A set of $\sim$ 5 medium bands ( $\sim$ 200 Å wide; a minimal set is Ca ii H&K plus Mg $b$ ) sensitive to stellar metallicity and surface gravity would map Local Group structure and formation over $\geq$ 70% of the sky, identifying streams, tidally stripped stars, and rare low-metallicity stars, and delivering a 3D distance map to the Milky Way’s virial radius, a probe of small-scale dark matter and first-star enrichment. The target is [Fe/H] to $\sim$ 10% and 90% dwarf/giant discrimination at $g\leq 25$ . Offset broad bands are shown to be insufficient here: the target features have equivalent widths of only $\sim$ 5–10 Å, requiring true medium bands even for faint stars. The transient-cadence cost (a 200 Å band needs $\sim$ 150 s versus 30 s to stay background-limited) is mitigated by making exposure time a function of filter wavelength. IBIS, Niji, and DESI Run 2 are the precursors that will validate the method.

#### Extended-baseline proper motions for halo dark matter

This is a case to probe the distribution of dark matter in the Milky Way halo through the kinematics of satellite dwarf galaxies, globular clusters, and stellar streams, in particular by detecting and modeling the gaps in tidal streams thought to be produced by encounters with dark-matter subhalos, thereby constraining the subhalo mass function. Because proper-motion accuracy improves as $t^{-3/2}$ with time baseline, continuing the survey past 2036 yields large astrometric gains: extending proper-motion accuracy to better than 0.5 mas yr-1 at or below $r\approx 24$ over the entire southern sky. Rubin will already have built a decade-long baseline over an area larger than Roman’s, and to depths not reached by planned astrometric surveys such as GaiaNIR, so additional epochs . : roughly ten to twenty broad-band epochs per year suffice to keep the baseline growing while allowing outlier rejection, and this case is the strongest argument for keeping some fraction of the post-LSST cadence in broad bands (the existing $ugrizy$ or the “offset” broad bands above) rather than moving entirely to medium or narrow bands, which motivates its placement in Group C. The prerequisite is a demonstration, using Gaia as a prior, that LSST can measure proper motions to the required accuracy for faint, low-proper-motion sources, plausibly by DR1 but perhaps requiring a longer baseline. It connects to the offset-broad-band and Galactic-archaeology cases above and to near-field cosmology programs.

#### Narrow-band H $\alpha$ emission-line imaging

An H $\alpha$ survey science from supernova remnants to the star-forming filaments of large-scale structure, bridging to 4MOST spectroscopy, exploiting Rubin’s unique combination of the widest field of view and active-optics-driven uniform image quality. It needs an H $\alpha$ filter or two ramp filters within the existing broadband range (potentially the largest narrow-band filter yet built), with DR1 setting the achievable redshift depth (focus on $z<1$ ); a possible Chilean tie-in is 4MOST-CHANCES.

#### Biosignature-proxy and Kuiper-belt-object triage

Two physics-based “triage” cases (explicitly not claims of detection) ask whether a single well-placed band sharpens a population-scale search. The first tests whether a $\sim$ 710 nm medium band (full width at half maximum, FWHM, 20–40 nm), $r$ and $i$ , can flag a vegetation-red-edge-like reflectance feature and separate it from haze/methane look-alikes, reducing the number of stacked detections needed to reach $3\sigma$ – $5\sigma$ ; the second tests whether a $\sim$ 450 nm blue-visible medium band (FWHM $\approx$ 60–80 nm) improves separation of organic-rich, ice-rich, mixed, and weakly active Kuiper-belt-object surface states beyond $ugrizy$ (figure of merit: $\geq$ 25% gain in the pairwise Mahalanobis distance at fixed cost). Both are framed as that concentrate scarce spectroscopy on the highest-information targets, and both to weather (near-simultaneous color pairs) and satellite-megaconstellation trails in the blue.

#### Exotic filter hardware

Three hardware concepts round out the group. The “butcher-block” segmented filter array would bond 21 uniform narrow-band tiles, one per charge-coupled-device (CCD) raft, into a single 75 cm element, giving each raft a clean, non-smeared bandpass the fast-beam smearing problem, sampling $\sim$ 21 redshift slices in one exposure with dithering (precedents: NASA “butcher-block” arrays, PAUCam). In addition to kilonovae detection, standard sirens from stellar-mass black holes detected by CE and ET could be observed using long-baseline monitoring of the sky areas of well-localized black-hole mergers for variability exceeding historical flares, adding a source of standard sirens that extends to larger cosmological distances.

### V.2 Bright sirens from LISA massive-black-hole mergers

LISA ( $\sim$ 2035) massive black-hole binary (MBHB) mergers ( $\sim$ 104–10 ${}^{8}\,M_{\odot}$ ) out to $z\sim 10$ , with localizations from tens of deg2 down to sub-deg2, evolving over before merger. A fraction of these mergers will occur in gas-rich circumbinary environments that can produce a detectable optical transient or quasi-periodic signature; Rubin could identify host candidates and extend the standard-siren Hubble diagram to a much longer cosmological lever arm. The case is for sustained, deep monitoring of LISA localization regions a robust photometric redshift catalog built from LSST/Roman/Euclid $\sim$ 1 Rubin-detectable EM counterpart per year (out to $z\sim 2$ –4, model-dependent) [29].

### V.3 Candidate hosts for the pulsar-timing-array background

In the nanohertz band, the maturing pulsar-timing-array (PTA) effort (NANOGrav, the European, Chinese, and Parkes arrays, MeerKAT, and ultimately the SKA) is expected by the mid-2030s to resolve both the anisotropy of the gravitational-wave background and a handful of individual nearby sources, predicted to be bright, inspiraling supermassive black-hole binaries (SMBHBs) superposed on a many-source background. Rubin’s depth and wide field can supply a catalog of candidate host galaxies for these nearby SMBHBs (expected to peak at $z\sim 0.1$ –1, or from associated AGN variability) to seed the single-source templates use in their searches. A confirmed association would characterize the bright foreground of the background and constrain SMBHB evolution, and even a null result is informative; the case requires only a sufficiently deep galaxy survey and no hardware change.

### V.4 A kilonova-demographics engine in the XG era

Beyond individual sirens, Rubin’s ToO system could build a large population of well-sampled kilonova light curves from the ET/CE catalog, resolving how ejecta mass, velocity, and composition depend on progenitor properties, moving beyond the single well-characterized event (GW170817) available today [30]. A population-level luminosity function, viewing-angle dependence, and ejecta-mass distribution can from a large photometric sample; this requires a distinct sub-day $griz$ rapid-cadence mode over the first $\sim$ 1–2 weeks post-merger for faint and distant kilonovae. Ejecta demographics feed nuclear-astrophysics ( $r$ -process) modeling, and at ET/CE rates automated light-curve classification and on-the-fly inference are required to triage which events warrant spectroscopy.

### V.5 Lensed binary-neutron-star mergers

Building on the census of $>$ 50,000 galaxy-scale lenses that LSST will assemble, Rubin’s ToO system could search for the optical counterparts of strongly lensed BNS mergers flagged by detectors. The era should raise the to $\sim$ 100 yr-1, with an estimated $\sim$ 0.1–3 lensed events per year; catching the rapidly-rising, intrinsically UV-bright kilonova (redshifted into the optical, where $u$ -band imaging aids discrimination from other transients) demands slewing and imaging within the first hour, exactly the rapid-response ToO capability this program builds. A single lensed multi-messenger detection would be transformative, extending standard-siren cosmology to $z\sim 1$ –2, well beyond the reach of unlensed events. No new hardware is required; the case connects to .

### V.6 Neutrino electromagnetic counterparts

By the mid-2030s, KM3NeT [2] and TRIDENT will open the Southern sky at TeV energies and IceCube-Gen2 [1] will ultra-high-energy ( $>$ 100 TeV) alerts, . At conventional energies (1–50 TeV) neutrino error boxes are large (0.8–7 deg2, up to 50 deg2 for cascades), which Rubin can blanket in a few pointings to deliver , using its $z/y$ -band depth to peer through dust. The needed change is a ToO scheduler protocol that promptly triggers low-latency $z/y$ imaging on a verified neutrino alert; a clean deep-Southern (a prior from early LSST) is required to . ; the case is framed as an argument that Rubin’s relevance to neutrino follow-up will grow as electromagnetic counterparts to neutrino signals are discovered.

### V.7 Galactic supernovae

With the , the group proposed to leverage Rubin Observatory for rapid electromagnetic follow-up of the next Galactic supernova, likely a core-collapse supernova (CCSN). This is a rare event ( $\sim$ 1–2 per century) that would enable unprecedented multimessenger characterization by combining neutrino, gravitational-wave, and optical data. The case has two parts: first, extending Rubin’s target-of-opportunity (ToO) capabilities beyond LSST to respond to neutrino alerts (from SNEWS Al Kharusi and others 3, DUNE DUNE Collaboration 20, and Hyper-K Bian and others 8), Rubin’s wide field of view and depth are essential for scanning the $\sim$ 2–25 deg2 localization regions these detectors provide and for catching faint or dust-obscured signals; second, building a dedicated all-sky rapid-response mode triggered by next-generation gravitational-wave detectors (, operational by the mid-2030s), since these could detect CCSNe anywhere on the sky, and only a Rubin response within minutes can capture the scientifically unique shock-breakout and pre-peak lightcurve evolution that serendipitous discovery cannot guarantee [7]. Both cases require modest additional development (leveraging existing LSST ToO infrastructure and strategies) and near-instantaneous autonomous scheduler overrides given the minutes-scale response window, and offer strong connections to neutrino/GW collaborations.

### V.8 White-dwarf binaries and the SN Ia progenitor problem with LISA

LISA will detect a large Galactic population of double-white-dwarf (DWD) and other ultra-compact binaries in the band, some with optical counterparts (eclipsing or AM CVn-type accreting systems). Cross-matching LISA sky localizations and orbital periods against Rubin’s alert stream and photometric archive, vetted with Gaia astrometry, spectroscopy, and archival catalogs, can identify and confirm these counterparts, building on the $\sim$ 50–75 systems expected to be found jointly by LISA and LSST. The signature outcome is a merging DWD detected by LISA that is spatially and temporally coincident with a Rubin-discovered SN Ia: a smoking-gun test of the double-degenerate progenitor channel and a direct measurement of the merger-to-explosion delay. Realizing it motivates continued rapid-ToO response and regular deep, high-cadence monitoring of the Galactic plane after LSST.

A cross-cutting outcome of the group is the need for direct, collaboration-level coordination of operational timelines between Rubin and the other major facilities (gravitational-wave and neutrino detectors, in particular): the community should avoid, for example, taking the main camera off-sky for a multi-year upgrade during a partner experiment’s planned multi-year observing run. The group also examined the impact of weather and climate at Cerro Pachón on post-LSST operations: multi-messenger are particularly vulnerable to weather losses, since a fading transient cannot be re-observed, and long-term climate trends (rising integrated water vapor and more frequent extreme El Niño events) should be folded into post-LSST scheduling and simulations.

## VI Group E: Enabling Technology and Upgrades
